qualification.title: OxfordAQA International Advanced Subsidiary Physics
summary: International AS Physics is a modular international qualification for study outside the United Kingdom.
The AS stage uses Unit 1 (Mechanics, materials and atoms) and Unit 2 (Electricity, waves and particles).
Each AS unit is a two-hour, 80-mark written paper worth 50% of AS and 20% of the full International A-level.
The Version 5.1 specification assesses practical knowledge through written papers rather than a separate practical examination.
AS content covers sections 3.1 to 3.5; sections 3.6 to 3.13 are International A-level only.

topic_guides.essence: Match each required physical quantity to its SI base unit and treat every prefix as an exact power-of-ten multiplier.
topic_guides.analogy: A prefix is a scale setting on a measuring instrument: the displayed number changes, but the physical quantity does not.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Convert 3.6 mg mm⁻³ into kg m⁻³.
worked_solution_steps: Convert the mass unit: 3.6 mg = 3.6 × 10⁻⁶ kg.
Convert the volume unit: 1 mm³ = (10⁻³ m)³ = 10⁻⁹ m³.
Divide using the converted units: 3.6 × 10⁻⁶ kg / 10⁻⁹ m³ = 3.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
State the result in standard SI form: 3.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not apply a prefix factor only once when the unit is squared or cubed.
checklist: The six base quantities required here are mass, length, time, amount of substance, thermodynamic temperature and electric current. Their SI base units are kilogram (kg), metre (m), second (s), mole (mol), kelvin (K) and ampere (A), respectively.

A prefix multiplies the unit by a power of ten: T = 10¹², G = 10⁹, M = 10⁶, k = 10³, c = 10⁻², m = 10⁻³, μ = 10⁻⁶, n = 10⁻⁹, p = 10⁻¹² and f = 10⁻¹⁵. Convert to the unprefixed SI unit before combining quantities in an equation.

A prefix applies to the whole unit symbol. For example, 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², not 10⁻³ m². Common derived units should also be recognised from base units, for example N = kg m s⁻² and J = kg m² s⁻². Candela definitions and dimensional analysis beyond these stated conversions are outside this AS scope.

Common derived units should also be recognised from base units, for example N = kg m s⁻² and J = kg m² s⁻². Candela definitions and dimensional analysis beyond these stated conversions are outside this AS scope.

topic_guides.essence: Convert energy units through fixed equality factors: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and 1 kW h = 3.60 × 10⁶ J.
topic_guides.analogy: Converting joules, electronvolts and kilowatt-hours is like expressing the same distance in metres, micrometres or kilometres.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A device transfers 0.75 kW h of energy. Calculate this energy in joules and in electronvolts.
worked_solution_steps: Use 1 kW h = 3.60 × 10⁶ J.
Use 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so energy in eV = (2.70 × 10⁶) / (1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹).
Energy = 1.69 × 10²⁵ eV, to three significant figures.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not treat kW h as a unit of power; the multiplication by time makes it a unit of energy.
checklist: The electronvolt is an energy unit: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Therefore convert eV to J by multiplying by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹, and J to eV by dividing by this value.

topic_guides.essence: Diagnose whether measurement quality is limited by scatter, bias or instrument resolution, then choose a remedy that addresses that cause.
topic_guides.analogy: Shots clustered away from a target are precise but systematically inaccurate; widely scattered shots show poor precision.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A balance reads 0.18 g when empty. Five readings of a sample are 12.42, 12.39, 12.44, 12.40 and 12.43 g. Identify the two error features and state suitable actions.
worked_solution_steps: The non-zero empty reading is a zero error and therefore a systematic error.
Correct each reading by subtracting 0.18 g, or re-zero/calibrate the balance before measuring.
The variation among the five readings is random error.
Repeat more readings and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of the random scatter; repetition alone would not remove the 0.18 g bias.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not claim that averaging removes a systematic error.
checklist: Random error causes readings to scatter unpredictably about a mean. Repeated measurements and averaging reduce its effect, although they do not remove the underlying variation.

Systematic error shifts readings consistently in one direction, for example through a zero error or poor calibration. Repetition does not remove it; the method or instrument must be checked, calibrated or corrected.

Precision describes the spread of repeated values, accuracy describes closeness to the accepted value, resolution is the smallest detectable change, repeatability uses the same method and operator, and reproducibility tests changed conditions such as operator or equipment.

topic_guides.essence: Express measurement tolerance as an absolute amount, a fraction or a percentage as required.
topic_guides.analogy: The uncertainty is a tolerance band around a measured value.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A length is (25.0 ± 0.2) cm. Calculate its percentage uncertainty.
worked_solution_steps: The absolute uncertainty is 0.2 cm and the measured length is 25.0 cm.
Fractional uncertainty = 0.2/25.0 = 0.008.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.008 × 100% = 0.8%.
Report 0.8% because percentage uncertainty has no physical unit.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not quote an absolute uncertainty as a percentage without dividing by the measured value.
checklist: Absolute uncertainty has the same unit as the measured quantity. Fractional uncertainty is Δx/x, and percentage uncertainty is (Δx/x) × 100%.
Use the uncertainty form that matches the question and keep the unit for an absolute uncertainty.
An uncertainty is a tolerance band around a measurement, not a second measurement.

topic_guides.essence: Match the uncertainty rule to the arithmetic operation: absolute for sums and differences, fractional for products, quotients and powers.
topic_guides.analogy: Each input contributes a margin; the operation decides whether margins add as amounts or proportions.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A rectangle has L = (12.4 ± 0.1) cm and W = (5.2 ± 0.1) cm. Find the percentage uncertainty in its area.
worked_solution_steps: Area A = LW, so multiplication requires fractional uncertainties.
Percentage uncertainty = 0.0273 × 100% = 2.73%.
The area has a percentage uncertainty of about 2.7%.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not add the two absolute length uncertainties when calculating the area.
checklist: For addition or subtraction, add absolute uncertainties. For multiplication or division, add fractional or percentage uncertainties.
If y = x^n, the fractional uncertainty in y is |n| times the fractional uncertainty in x.

topic_guides.essence: Use error bars and acceptable limiting lines to estimate uncertainty in a graph gradient or intercept.
topic_guides.analogy: The best-fit line is one plausible model; limiting lines show the allowed range of models.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Best-fit, steepest and shallowest gradients are 2.40, 2.75 and 2.10 N m⁻¹. Find the gradient uncertainty.
worked_solution_steps: The full gradient range is 2.75 - 2.10 = 0.65 N m⁻¹.
Use half the full range for the uncertainty estimate.
Gradient uncertainty = 0.65/2 = 0.325 N m⁻¹.
Report approximately (2.40 ± 0.33) N m⁻¹.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use point scatter alone as the gradient uncertainty without acceptable limiting lines.
checklist: Error bars show the range of plausible values for each measured point. Draw them using the relevant uncertainty.
For a straight-line graph, draw acceptable steepest and shallowest lines through the error bars. Gradient or intercept uncertainty is commonly half the full range.

Use the same axes, units and plotted quantities for the best-fit and limiting lines. If error bars are not supplied, use the stated instrument uncertainty or the scatter of repeated measurements to estimate a defensible vertical and horizontal range; do not invent numerical error bars that the data do not support.

topic_guides.essence: Reduce a physical situation to defensible approximate values and powers of ten, then keep only the scale justified by those assumptions.
topic_guides.analogy: An order-of-magnitude estimate is a map viewed from high altitude: it shows scale and direction, not street-level detail.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Estimate the order of magnitude of the mass of air in a classroom 8 m long, 6 m wide and 3 m high. Take air density as 1 kg m⁻³.
worked_solution_steps: Estimate the room volume: V ≈ 8 × 6 × 3 ≈ 1.4 × 10² m³.
Use m = ρV with ρ ≈ 1 kg m⁻³.
The estimated mass is m ≈ 1 × 1.4 × 10² ≈ 1.4 × 10² kg.
The coefficient 1.4 is below √10, so the nearest order of magnitude is 10² kg.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not give several significant figures when the input values were only rough estimates.
checklist: An order of magnitude is a power of ten. Write the estimate in standard form and choose the nearest power of ten rather than preserving unjustified detail.
A useful estimate combines simple geometric or physical assumptions with familiar benchmark values. State assumptions so that the reasoning can be assessed.
For a value a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10, the nearest order of magnitude is 10ⁿ when a < √10 and 10ⁿ⁺¹ when a > √10.

topic_guides.essence: Equilibrium requires zero resultant force, so horizontal and vertical components balance even when individual forces are non-zero.
topic_guides.analogy: A balanced tug has forces present in both directions but no acceleration.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 50 N weight is supported by an inclined cable at 35° above the horizontal and a horizontal cable. Find the inclined-cable tension.
worked_solution_steps: The angle is measured above the horizontal, so the vertical component of the inclined tension is T sin 35°.
Only the inclined cable supplies an upward component, so set T sin 35° = 50 N for vertical equilibrium.
T = 50/sin 35° = 87 N, to two significant figures.
The horizontal cable balances the horizontal component; this is consistent with ΣF_x = 0.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not conclude that equilibrium means zero velocity.

topic_guides.essence: Rotational effect is force times perpendicular lever arm; rotational equilibrium balances clockwise and anticlockwise moments.
topic_guides.analogy: A door opens more easily at the handle because the perpendicular lever arm is larger.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 200 N beam weight acts 2.0 m from a hinge. An upward force acts 4.0 m from the hinge. Find the force for equilibrium.
worked_solution_steps: Take moments about the hinge so hinge force has zero moment.
Clockwise moment = 200 × 2.0 = 400 N m.
Set F × 4.0 = 400 N m.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use a non-perpendicular distance as the lever arm.
checklist: The moment of a force about a point is Fd⊥, where d⊥ is the perpendicular distance to the force line of action.
A couple consists of equal, opposite coplanar forces; its resultant is zero but its moment is one force times the separation.
For rotational equilibrium, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments about any point.

topic_guides.essence: Use directed changes for displacement, velocity and acceleration, and distinguish an interval average from a value at one instant.
topic_guides.analogy: Average velocity describes the whole trip with one arrow; instantaneous velocity is the reading at one precise moment.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A runner completes one 400 m lap in 80 s and finishes at the starting point. Find the average speed and average velocity.
worked_solution_steps: The total distance travelled is 400 m.
Average speed = distance/time = 400/80 = 5.0 m s⁻¹.
The final position equals the initial position, so displacement is 0 m.
Average velocity = displacement/time = 0/80 = 0 m s⁻¹.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use total distance when calculating average velocity.

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = Δv/Δt. Acceleration and velocity may have opposite signs when an object is slowing down.
Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at one moment and may be obtained from the gradient of a tangent to a displacement-time graph.

topic_guides.analogy: A gradient tells how fast the next quantity is being produced, while an area totals everything produced over an interval.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A velocity-time graph rises uniformly from 2.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 8.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 3.0 s. Find the acceleration and displacement.
worked_solution_steps: Acceleration is the graph gradient: a = (8.0 - 2.0)/3.0 = 2.0 m s⁻².
Displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph.
Use the trapezium area: s = ½(2.0 + 8.0) × 3.0.
The displacement is 15 m.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not call the area under a displacement-time graph a standard kinematic quantity; velocity comes from its gradient.
checklist: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity. A curved graph has changing velocity, and its instantaneous velocity is the gradient of a tangent.
The gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration, while the signed area between the graph and the time axis is displacement.
The signed area under an acceleration-time graph is change in velocity. Areas below the time axis contribute negatively.

topic_guides.essence: For constant acceleration, define a direction, assign signs consistently and choose the equation that links the available data directly to the target.
topic_guides.analogy: The four equations are different views of the same constant-acceleration motion, each omitting one variable.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes uniformly at 4.0 m s⁻². Calculate its stopping distance.
worked_solution_steps: Choose the initial direction as positive: u = 20 m s⁻¹, v = 0 and a = -4.0 m s⁻².
Time is not given or required, so use v² = u² + 2as.
Substitute: 0² = 20² + 2(-4.0)s.
Solve to obtain s = 50 m.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use these equations when acceleration varies with time.
checklist: The equations v = u + at, s = (u + v)t/2, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as apply only when acceleration is constant.
Choose a positive direction before assigning signs. Quantities directed opposite to that axis, including acceleration or displacement, are negative.
Select the equation containing the known quantities and the required unknown; avoid introducing an unnecessary extra unknown.

topic_guides.essence: Linearise free fall as s against t² so that many measurements yield g from twice the best-fit gradient.
topic_guides.analogy: Squaring the time straightens the curved free-fall relationship, turning g into a measurable graph gradient.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A best-fit graph of fall distance s against t² has gradient 4.82 m s⁻². Determine g.
worked_solution_steps: For release from rest, s = ½gt².
Compare with y = mx: the gradient of s against t² is g/2.
Therefore g = 2 × gradient = 2 × 4.82 m s⁻².
The measured gravitational field strength is g = 9.64 m s⁻².
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not report the gradient of an s-against-t² graph as g; it equals g/2.
checklist: For an object released from rest and falling with negligible drag, s = ½gt². A graph of s against t² should therefore be a straight line through the origin with gradient g/2.
Measure a range of fall distances and corresponding times rather than calculating g from one reading. Repeats reduce timing scatter.
The measured distance must correspond to the object's displacement during the timed interval. Automatic timing such as light gates reduces reaction-time error.

topic_guides.essence: Split projectile motion into constant horizontal velocity and uniformly accelerated vertical motion, linked by a common time.
topic_guides.analogy: A projectile performs two motions at once: a steady sideways glide and an independent vertical fall.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal. Neglect air resistance and take g = 9.81 m s⁻². Find the time to reach maximum height and the horizontal distance travelled in that time.
worked_solution_steps: Resolve the initial velocity: u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹ and u_x = 20 cos 30° = 17.3 m s⁻¹.
At maximum height v_y = 0. Using v_y = u_y - gt gives t = 10/9.81 = 1.02 s.
Horizontal speed is constant, so x = u_x t.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not apply g to the horizontal component when air resistance is neglected.
checklist: In a uniform gravitational field with negligible air resistance, horizontal and vertical motions are independent but share the same time.
Resolve an initial speed u at angle θ into u_x = u cos θ and u_y = u sin θ. Horizontal acceleration is zero and vertical acceleration is g downward.
Apply the uniform-acceleration equations separately in each direction. Horizontal velocity remains constant, while vertical velocity changes uniformly.

topic_guides.essence: As speed changes, fluid forces change the resultant force until a possible balance produces constant terminal or maximum speed.
topic_guides.analogy: Moving faster through air is like pushing through increasingly resistant water: the opposing force grows until it can match the driving force.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A skydiver of mass 75 kg falls at constant terminal speed. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². State the drag force and explain what happens immediately after the parachute opens.
worked_solution_steps: At terminal speed, acceleration is zero, so the resultant force is zero.
The weight is mg = 75 × 9.8 = 735 N downward.
Therefore the drag force is 735 N upward at the original terminal speed.
Opening the parachute greatly increases drag so drag initially exceeds weight; the resultant is upward and the downward speed decreases until a new, lower terminal speed is reached.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not say that forces are absent at terminal speed; weight and drag are present and balanced.
checklist: Drag is a resistive force opposite relative motion through a fluid, and it generally increases with speed. Friction similarly opposes relative motion between surfaces.
Lift acts approximately perpendicular to the relative airflow and can support an aircraft or alter a vehicle's normal force and grip.
A falling object reaches terminal speed when the upward drag balances its weight. The resultant force and acceleration are then zero, although velocity remains non-zero.
Air resistance makes a projectile path non-symmetric and reduces range and maximum height. A vehicle's maximum steady speed occurs when its driving force equals the total resistance.

topic_guides.essence: Relate motion to the resultant external force, and keep third-law force pairs on their two separate interacting bodies.
topic_guides.analogy: A free-body diagram is an account for one object: only forces acting on that object belong in its force total.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 1200 kg car has a driving force of 3000 N and resistive forces totalling 900 N. Find its acceleration and identify the third-law partner to the road's forward force on the tyres.
worked_solution_steps: Calculate the forward resultant force: ΣF = 3000 - 900 = 2100 N.
Use ΣF = ma because the car's mass is constant.
The third-law partner is the tyres' backward force on the road; it acts on the road, not on the car.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not pair weight with the normal contact force as a Newton's third-law pair; both act on the same object.
checklist: Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant external force.
Newton's second law states that resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum. For constant mass this becomes ΣF = ma.

Newton's third law pairs forces of the same type acting on different interacting bodies. The forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and simultaneous, so they do not cancel on one free-body diagram.

topic_guides.essence: Track momentum with signs across an isolated interaction, then use kinetic energy separately to classify the collision.
topic_guides.analogy: Momentum is redistributed among objects like a fixed signed total, even when kinetic energy changes form.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 0.40 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 0.60 kg trolley and they stick together. Find their common speed and classify the collision.
worked_solution_steps: Initial momentum = 0.40 × 3.0 + 0.60 × 0 = 1.2 kg m s⁻¹.
The combined mass after collision is 0.40 + 0.60 = 1.00 kg.
Conservation of momentum gives 1.2 = 1.00v, so v = 1.2 m s⁻¹ in the original direction.
Because the trolleys stick together and kinetic energy decreases, the collision is perfectly inelastic.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not assume kinetic energy is conserved in every collision; momentum conservation is the general isolated-system rule.
checklist: Linear momentum is p = mv and is a vector. Assign a positive direction so that objects moving oppositely have momenta with opposite signs.
Total momentum is conserved in an isolated system: total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after it. External impulse must be negligible over the interaction time.

An elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy as well as momentum. An inelastic collision conserves momentum but transfers some kinetic energy to other stores; if objects stick together, it is perfectly inelastic.
In an explosion, initially stored energy becomes kinetic energy, while the momenta of the fragments still sum to the initial momentum.

topic_guides.essence: Impulse accumulates force over time and produces exactly the corresponding vector change in momentum.
topic_guides.analogy: A brief large push and a longer small push can deliver the same impulse if their force-time areas are equal.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A force on a ball rises linearly from zero to 600 N in 4.0 ms and then falls linearly to zero over the next 2.0 ms. Find the impulse.
worked_solution_steps: The force-time region is a triangle with total base 6.0 ms = 6.0 × 10⁻³ s.
Impulse equals the graph area: J = ½ × base × height.
Therefore the ball's momentum changes by 1.8 kg m s⁻¹ in the force direction.
topic_guides.pitfall: Convert milliseconds to seconds before calculating an impulse in N s.
checklist: Resultant force is the rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt for a constant average force, or the instantaneous gradient dp/dt conceptually.
Impulse J equals change in momentum, J = Δp, and also equals FΔt for constant force.
For a varying force, impulse is the signed area under the force-time graph. Its unit N s is equivalent to kg m s⁻¹.

topic_guides.essence: When momentum change is fixed, extending collision time reduces average force.
topic_guides.analogy: Catching an egg by moving your hands backward gives the same stop but spreads it over a longer time.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 0.15 kg ball travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ is stopped. Compare the average force if the stopping time is 0.010 s or 0.050 s.
worked_solution_steps: The magnitude of momentum change is Δp = mv = 0.15 × 20 = 3.0 kg m s⁻¹.
For 0.010 s, average force = 3.0/0.010 = 300 N.
For 0.050 s, average force = 3.0/0.050 = 60 N.
Increasing contact time by a factor of five reduces the average force by a factor of five.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not state that a crumple zone reduces the car's momentum change when the car still comes to rest.
checklist: For a fixed change in momentum, average force is F = Δp/Δt. Increasing the time over which an object is brought to rest reduces the average force.
Crumple zones, airbags, helmets, packaging and landing mats deform to extend stopping time. They do not remove the momentum change; they reduce the force associated with it.
A real impact force is often variable, so the force-time area remains the impulse. Safety features generally lower and broaden the force-time pulse.

topic_guides.essence: Work measures energy transfer by the component of force along displacement, or equivalently the area under F against s.
topic_guides.analogy: Only the part of a push pointing along the path moves the object forward; a sideways push does no work along that path.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 40 N force pulls a box 5.0 m along a floor at 60° above the horizontal. Calculate the work done by this force.
worked_solution_steps: The displacement is horizontal, so use the horizontal component of the force.
W = Fs cos θ = 40 × 5.0 × cos 60°.
The work done by the 40 N force is 1.0 × 10² J.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use the full force in W = Fs unless force and displacement are parallel.
checklist: Work done by a constant force is W = Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. Only the component parallel to displacement transfers energy by work.
The area under a force-displacement graph equals work done, including when the force varies. Calculate areas from the graph shape and axis scales.
Work is a scalar measured in joules. A force perpendicular to displacement has zero work because cos 90° = 0.

topic_guides.essence: Power describes how quickly energy is transferred; efficiency compares the useful part with the total input.
topic_guides.analogy: Two pumps may transfer the same total water, but the one that does it sooner has greater power.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A lift raises a 600 kg load vertically at constant speed 1.5 m s⁻¹. Its input power is 12 kW. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². Find useful output power and efficiency.
worked_solution_steps: At constant speed, lifting force equals weight: F = mg = 600 × 9.8 = 5880 N.
Useful power = Fv = 5880 × 1.5 = 8820 W.
Efficiency = useful output/input = 8820/12000 = 0.735.
The efficiency is 73.5%, or 74% to two significant figures.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not calculate efficiency from useful output divided by wasted output; the denominator is total input.
checklist: Power is the rate of energy transfer or work done: P = ΔW/Δt. At constant velocity with a force parallel to motion, P = Fv.
For a varying force or speed, instantaneous power is the product of force and velocity components parallel to one another. Average power is total work divided by total time.
Efficiency = useful output power/input power, or the equivalent energy ratio for the same process. It has no unit and is commonly expressed as a percentage.

topic_guides.essence: Account for energy transfer between defined initial and final states, using mgh and ½mv² with a consistent height reference.
topic_guides.analogy: Energy accounting is a balanced ledger: an amount leaving one store must appear in another store or in the surroundings.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 0.50 kg ball is released from rest 12 m above the ground. Ignore air resistance. Find its speed just before reaching the ground.
worked_solution_steps: Initial gravitational potential energy relative to the ground is mgh = 0.50 × 9.8 × 12.
The ball starts from rest, so its initial kinetic energy is zero.
Conservation of energy gives mgh = ½mv²; mass cancels.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use mgh as an absolute energy without specifying a reference height; only changes in gravitational potential energy are physical.
checklist: Energy is conserved: it cannot be created or destroyed, but it can be transferred between stores or to the surroundings by work, heating, radiation or electrical transfer.
The change in gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is ΔE_p = mgΔh. Kinetic energy is E_k = ½mv².

Choose clear initial and final states, then equate the energy decrease from one store with the energy increase in other stores when transfers to the surroundings are negligible or included explicitly.

topic_guides.essence: Use conservation of energy while explicitly including work against resistance and any elastic store involved.
topic_guides.analogy: A resistive force is an energy diversion: some energy that could have become motion is instead spread as heating to the surroundings.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 2.0 kg crate descends 3.0 m and reaches 6.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the work done against resistive forces. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
worked_solution_steps: The loss of gravitational potential energy is mgh = 2.0 × 9.8 × 3.0 = 58.8 J.
The gain in kinetic energy is ½mv² = ½ × 2.0 × 6.0² = 36.0 J.
Energy transferred against resistance = 58.8 - 36.0.
The work done against resistive forces is 22.8 J.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not set mgh equal to ½mv² when resistance has done work.
checklist: When a resistive force acts opposite to motion, work is done against it. This transfers energy from moving or gravitational stores to internal energy stores of the object and surroundings.

An elastic object stores energy when stretched or compressed within its elastic behaviour. In an ideal return, that elastic potential energy can transfer back to kinetic or gravitational potential energy.
A complete energy equation includes every relevant transfer: for example, loss of gravitational potential energy = gain in kinetic energy + work done against resistance.

topic_guides.essence: Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V, and must be calculated with consistent SI units.
topic_guides.analogy: Density asks how much matter is packed into each unit of space.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A metal sample has mass 0.540 kg and volume 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Find density.
worked_solution_steps: Use ρ = m/V.
Substitute ρ = 0.540/(2.0 × 10⁻⁴).
State the result to an appropriate number of significant figures.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not mix cm³ and m³ without conversion.
checklist: Density is mass per unit volume: ρ = m/V, with SI unit kg m⁻³.
For a uniform sample, mass and volume change in the same ratio when the amount changes.
Density compares how much matter occupies a given space, so dimensions must be converted consistently before calculation.

topic_guides.essence: Within the proportional region, extension is proportional to force and F = kΔL, where k measures stiffness.
topic_guides.analogy: A stiffer spring needs more force for the same extension.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A spring extends 4.0 cm under a 6.0 N load within its proportional region. Find k.
worked_solution_steps: Convert extension: ΔL = 4.0 cm = 0.040 m.
Use F = kΔL.
The spring constant is 150 N m⁻¹.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use centimetres when k is required in N m⁻¹.
checklist: Hooke's law states that extension is proportional to force up to the limit of proportionality.
For a spring in this region, F = kΔL, where k is stiffness in N m⁻¹; larger k means a stiffer spring.
The elastic limit is the greatest load for which the object returns to its original length; it is distinct from the limit of proportionality.
This topic covers the force-extension model, while density is treated separately even though both appear in the official bulk-properties statement.

topic_guides.essence: Stress and strain normalise force and extension by original dimensions; breaking stress is stress at fracture.
topic_guides.analogy: Stress is like pressure, comparing force with the area over which it acts.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A wire has area 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² and original length 2.0 m. It carries 120 N and extends 1.5 mm; it fractures at 200 N. Calculate the tensile stress, strain at 120 N and breaking stress.
worked_solution_steps: Tensile stress at 120 N: σ = F/A = 120/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 6.0 × 10⁷ Pa.
Convert extension: ΔL = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m, so ε = ΔL/L = 1.5 × 10⁻³/2.0 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴.
Breaking stress uses the fracture force: σ_break = 200/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.0 × 10⁸ Pa.
Stress is measured in Pa; strain is dimensionless. Elastic strain energy is a separate force-extension area calculation.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use stretched length or changed area in the AS definitions.
checklist: Tensile stress is σ = F/A and tensile strain is ε = ΔL/L, using original area and length; strain has no unit.
Breaking stress is the tensile stress at fracture and allows fair comparison of specimens with different dimensions.
Stress and strain separate material behaviour from sample size; elastic strain energy is treated in the adjacent energy topic.
You can calculate tensile stress, tensile strain and breaking stress with correct dimensions and units.

topic_guides.essence: Elastic strain energy is recoverable energy stored during elastic deformation and equals the force-extension area.
topic_guides.analogy: Stretching a material stores energy like compressing a spring.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A wire is stretched by 1.5 mm under a 120 N force in its linear region. Find stored elastic energy.
worked_solution_steps: Convert extension: ΔL = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m.
The linear force-extension graph forms a triangle.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use ½FΔL for a non-linear graph without finding the actual area.
checklist: Elastic strain energy is stored when deformation is elastic and can be recovered on unloading.
It equals the area under a force-extension graph. For a linear region, E = ½FΔL.
The triangular formula applies only when force rises linearly from zero.
You can calculate stored elastic energy and interpret force-extension areas.

topic_guides.essence: Read graph regions as changes in material response: proportional, elastic, plastic and fracture are distinct ideas.
topic_guides.analogy: A material graph records response as demand rises, from recoverable deformation to permanent change and eventual failure.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A wire is loaded beyond its elastic limit but below fracture, then unloaded. Describe the unloading result and the material behaviour demonstrated.
worked_solution_steps: The wire was taken beyond its elastic limit, so complete recovery is no longer possible.
On unloading, extension decreases because the material still has elastic response.
The wire does not return to its original length.
The remaining extension is permanent plastic deformation.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not treat the limit of proportionality and elastic limit as interchangeable labels.
checklist: On a force-extension graph, the initial straight section is the proportional region. Beyond it, extension may still be elastic until the elastic limit; after that limit, permanent plastic deformation remains when load is removed.
Fracture is the point where the specimen breaks. A brittle material fractures with little plastic deformation, whereas a ductile material shows substantial plastic extension before fracture.
Stress-strain graphs permit comparison between materials of different dimensions. Their initial gradient is Young modulus for a linear elastic material.

topic_guides.essence: Young modulus quantifies stiffness through the ratio of stress to strain in the linear elastic region.
topic_guides.analogy: Young modulus compares how much a material yields under the same stress, independent of sample length and thickness.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A wire of length 2.0 m and area 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ m² extends by 0.80 mm under a 90 N force. Find Young modulus.
worked_solution_steps: Convert the extension: ΔL = 0.80 mm = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m.
Use E = FL/(AΔL).
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use the gradient of a force-extension graph directly as Young modulus; it gives spring constant unless dimensions are included.
checklist: Young modulus is tensile stress divided by tensile strain: E = σ/ε = FL/(AΔL). It is measured in pascals and is a property of the material in its linear elastic region.
A large Young modulus means a material is stiff: it produces a small strain for a given stress. It does not necessarily mean that the material is strong or difficult to fracture.
On a stress-strain graph, Young modulus is the gradient of the initial straight-line section.

topic_guides.essence: A valid Young modulus practical measures small extensions and dimensions accurately, stays in the linear elastic region and uses a graph-based gradient.
topic_guides.analogy: The experiment magnifies a tiny material response: length makes extension visible, while careful diameter measurement controls a squared uncertainty.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A student measures one diameter once, uses a 20 cm wire and loads it until the graph curves. Give three improvements and explain each.
worked_solution_steps: Measure diameter at several positions and perpendicular directions with a micrometer and use the mean; this reduces scatter and reveals non-uniformity.
Use a longer wire with a fiducial marker and scale; larger extension reduces percentage uncertainty and parallax can be controlled.
Restrict analysis to the straight-line load-extension region so Hooke's law and E remain valid.
Use a best-fit graph gradient rather than one pair of readings to reduce the influence of random scatter.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not load the wire beyond its elastic limit and then use all points in one straight-line calculation.
checklist: Measure original wire length L, diameter at several positions and orientations with a micrometer, then calculate A = πd²/4 using the mean diameter.
Increase load in measured steps within the elastic range, record extension with a fiducial marker and scale, avoid parallax and repeat readings. Plot force-extension or stress-strain data.
Use a long, thin wire for measurable extension, secure the apparatus, check zero errors and stop before the elastic limit. A best-fit graph reduces random scatter.

topic_guides.essence: Use the pattern of Rutherford scattering outcomes as evidence for a small, dense, positively charged nucleus and mostly empty atomic space.
topic_guides.analogy: Most particles pass through because an atom is a vast sparse region with a tiny but strongly repulsive centre.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Explain why a very small fraction of alpha particles were scattered through angles greater than 90°.
worked_solution_steps: An alpha particle is positively charged.
A large deflection requires a strong repulsive electrostatic force.
Such a force occurs only near a concentrated positive charge.
Therefore the atom contains a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not attribute the large-angle scattering to electrons; their mass and distribution cannot produce the observed strong deflections.
checklist: Atoms contain a small, positively charged nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Most atomic volume is empty space.

Most alpha particles pass through thin foil with little deflection, showing empty space. A small fraction deflect through large angles or rebound, showing that positive charge and most mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Scientific models change when new evidence cannot be explained by the previous model; nuclear structure developed through successive scattering and particle observations.

topic_guides.essence: Read A and Z precisely, conserve them in nuclear equations and calculate specific charge as charge per kilogram.
topic_guides.analogy: A counts everyone in the nucleus while Z counts only protons, which define the element's identity.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: For ^23_11Na^+, state protons, neutrons and electrons, then calculate the magnitude of electron specific charge using e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and m_e = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
worked_solution_steps: Z = 11, so the ion has 11 protons.
Neutrons = A - Z = 23 - 11 = 12.
A +1 ion has lost one electron, so it has 10 electrons.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not confuse nucleon number with neutron number; neutrons are A - Z.
checklist: A proton has charge +e, a neutron has zero charge and an electron has charge -e. Proton number Z counts protons; nucleon number A counts protons plus neutrons.
Nuclide notation ^A_ZX identifies element X. Neutron number is A - Z, and a neutral atom has Z electrons; an ion has gained or lost electrons.

Specific charge is charge divided by mass, q/m, in C kg⁻¹. Compare the net charge and mass of the object: a proton has +e/m_p, a fully ionised nucleus has +Ze divided by its nuclear mass, and an ion has the net charge left after electron loss or gain divided by the ion mass. State the sign when direction matters and the magnitude when comparing how large the specific charge is. Atomic mass unit recall is not required at AS.

topic_guides.essence: Recognise particle-antiparticle pairs by matching mass and opposing relevant properties, especially charge.
topic_guides.analogy: An antiparticle is a matched counterpart: the same mass label, but an opposite charge sign where charge is present.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: State the antiparticle of electron, proton, neutron and neutrino. Compare a positron with an electron.
worked_solution_steps: Electron → positron; proton → antiproton.
Neutron → antineutron; neutrino → antineutrino.
A positron has charge +e whereas an electron has charge -e.
They have equal mass.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not call a positron a positively charged proton; it is the antiparticle of the electron.
checklist: Classify particles by their properties and interactions, and recognise that every particle has a corresponding antiparticle.

An antiparticle has the same mass as its particle partner but opposite charge where the particle is charged. Required examples include positron/electron, antiproton/proton, antineutron/neutron and antineutrino/neutrino.
Neutral particles can still have distinct antiparticles, so charge alone is not enough to identify every pair.

topic_guides.topic_title: Annihilation, pair production and rest energy
topic_guides.essence: Annihilation and pair production convert between particle rest energy and other forms while conserving charge and momentum.
topic_guides.analogy: Pair production is energy paying the entry cost for two equal-mass particles; annihilation returns that account to other products.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An electron and positron at rest annihilate. State charge before and after and explain the product momentum condition.
worked_solution_steps: Initial total charge is -e + e = 0.
Equal rest masses provide their combined rest energy to the products.
If initially at rest, total initial momentum is zero.
Products must have total charge zero and total momentum zero; photons emitted in opposite directions satisfy both conditions.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not describe pair production as creation of one particle only; an antiparticle is required to conserve charge.
checklist: In annihilation, a particle and antiparticle transform their rest energy and any kinetic energy into other particles or photons while conservation laws are satisfied.
Pair production creates a particle and its antiparticle from sufficient energy. A nearby nucleus or other body may take recoil so momentum is conserved; minimum energy supplies both rest energies.
Particle and antiparticle have equal mass and rest energy. Rest energy is commonly expressed in MeV; E = mc² calculations are not required at AS.

topic_guides.essence: Write nuclear decay equations by conserving nucleon number and charge, including the correct neutrino species.
topic_guides.analogy: A nuclear equation is a strict inventory: total nucleons and total charge must balance on both sides.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Complete: ^14_6C → ____ + ____ + antineutrino.
worked_solution_steps: In beta-minus decay, A remains 14.
Z increases from 6 to 7, so the daughter is ^14_7N.
The emitted beta-minus particle is an electron, ^0_-1e.
Thus ^14_6C → ^14_7N + ^0_-1e + antineutrino.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not omit the neutrino or antineutrino from a beta-decay equation.

topic_guides.essence: Use repeated halving at equal time intervals and distinguish the number of half-lives from elapsed time.
topic_guides.analogy: Each half-life removes half of what remains, not half of the original amount each time.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A source has activity 960 Bq and half-life 6.0 h. Find its activity after 18 h.
worked_solution_steps: Number of half-lives n = 18/6.0 = 3.
After one half-life: 960/2 = 480 Bq.
After two and three half-lives: 240 Bq then 120 Bq.
The activity after 18 h is 120 Bq.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not subtract the same numerical amount after each half-life; radioactive decay is exponential.
checklist: Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei, count rate or activity to fall to half its current value. It is constant for a given isotope under unchanged conditions.
On a decay graph, choose a convenient activity or count rate and find the interval to half that value; the first plotted point need not be the exact initial value.
For whole-number half-lives, remaining quantity = initial quantity × (1/2)^n, where n is elapsed time divided by half-life.

topic_guides.topic_title: Nuclear excited states and gamma emission
topic_guides.essence: Gamma emission is a transition between nuclear energy states with no change in proton or nucleon number.
topic_guides.analogy: An excited nucleus drops to a lower energy step by releasing a gamma photon.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Explain why technetium-99m can be detected during imaging without changing the patient's element composition.
worked_solution_steps: Technetium-99m is an excited nuclear state.
It emits gamma photons when moving to a lower nuclear energy state.
Photons leave the body and are detected externally.
A and Z do not change, so the element remains technetium.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not describe gamma emission as alpha or beta decay.
checklist: An excited nucleus has excess energy. Gamma emission occurs when it falls to a lower nuclear energy state, so A and Z remain unchanged.
Technetium-99m is useful in imaging because gamma radiation is detected outside the body and its half-life is suitably short.
Gamma emission changes nuclear energy, not nuclear composition.

topic_guides.topic_title: Alpha, beta and gamma properties and applications
topic_guides.essence: Compare radiation by ionisation, penetration, absorption, hazard and practical use rather than by one property alone.
topic_guides.analogy: Radiation choice is a trade-off between how strongly it ionises and how far it travels.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Match a suitable radiation to each thickness measurement: very thin paper, aluminium foil and thick steel. Explain why the other choices are less suitable in each case.
worked_solution_steps: Use alpha for very thin paper: it is absorbed strongly, so a small change in paper thickness gives a useful count change.
Use beta for aluminium foil: its intermediate penetration allows a measurable transmitted count while remaining sensitive to thickness.
Use gamma for thick steel: its high penetration allows radiation to reach the detector through a substantial thickness.
State the practical trade-off: the source must be neither stopped completely nor transmitted with almost no change.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not assign beta automatically to paper or rank hazard by penetration alone; match the radiation to material thickness and exposure route.
checklist: Alpha is strongly ionising and weakly penetrating, beta has intermediate penetration and ionisation, and gamma is weakly ionising but highly penetrating.
Hazard depends on radiation type, source location, activity, exposure time and shielding; penetration alone does not determine risk.

Thickness measurements use a source matched to the material: alpha can monitor very thin paper, beta can monitor aluminium foil, and gamma can monitor thicker steel because the detector count changes measurably through the material.
You can compare penetration, absorption, hazards and applications without treating the three radiations as interchangeable.

topic_guides.essence: Correct for background and control geometry before testing the inverse-square relationship between gamma count rate and distance.
topic_guides.analogy: The same radiation spreads over the surface of an expanding sphere, so each square metre receives less as distance increases.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A detector records 500 counts min⁻¹ at 0.50 m from a gamma source. Background is 20 counts min⁻¹. Predict the measured count rate at 1.0 m.
worked_solution_steps: Corrected source count rate at 0.50 m = 500 - 20 = 480 counts min⁻¹.
Doubling distance reduces source count rate by 2² = 4.
Corrected source count rate at 1.0 m = 480/4 = 120 counts min⁻¹.
Add background back: predicted measured rate = 120 + 20 = 140 counts min⁻¹.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not apply the inverse-square law directly to uncorrected counts when background is significant.
checklist: For an isotropic point source with negligible absorption, intensity I follows I ∝ 1/r². Doubling distance reduces intensity to one quarter.
To verify the law with gamma radiation, keep source activity, detector orientation, counting time and intervening material constant while varying distance. Plot corrected count rate against 1/r².
Background radiation adds counts not produced by the source. Measure background for a comparable time, convert to count rate and subtract it before testing the relationship.

topic_guides.essence: Current measures charge flow rate, potential difference measures energy per charge and resistance links them for stated conditions.
topic_guides.analogy: Charge is the amount delivered, current is delivery rate and potential difference is the energy supplied to each coulomb.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 12 V supply transfers 360 J through a resistor in 30 s. Calculate charge, current and resistance.
worked_solution_steps: Use V = W/Q, so Q = W/V = 360/12 = 30 C.
The resistance is 12 Ω.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not define potential difference as energy per unit time; that is related to power.
checklist: Current is rate of flow of charge: I = ΔQ/Δt. Conventional current is defined in the direction positive charge would move.
Potential difference is work done or energy transferred per unit charge: V = W/Q. It measures energy transferred between two points per coulomb.
Resistance is the ratio of potential difference to current for a component at a stated condition: R = V/I. Its unit is the ohm, Ω.

topic_guides.essence: Read the shape of an I-V characteristic as evidence of whether resistance remains constant or changes with temperature, bias or material behaviour.
topic_guides.analogy: An ohmic conductor behaves like a constant-width pipe, while a filament lamp effectively narrows as heating increases resistance.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A filament lamp's I-against-V graph becomes less steep as p.d. increases. Explain what happens to its resistance.
worked_solution_steps: On an I-against-V graph, gradient is I/V.
For a component, R = V/I, so resistance is the reciprocal of I/V.
A less steep graph has smaller I/V.
Therefore V/I is larger: filament resistance increases as it becomes hotter.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not claim that every straight line on an I-V plot demonstrates Ohm's law without checking the origin and constant conditions.
checklist: An ohmic conductor at constant physical conditions has I ∝ V, producing a straight-line I-V graph through the origin and constant resistance.
A filament lamp has increasing resistance as current increases because its temperature rises; its I-against-V graph becomes less steep.
A semiconductor diode conducts very little in reverse bias and below its forward threshold, then current rises rapidly in forward bias. Its resistance is not constant.
Ohm's law is the special relationship I ∝ V only when physical conditions, particularly temperature, remain constant.

Its resistance is not constant, and one short exam-action label on each branch.

topic_guides.essence: An ideal ammeter is zero resistance in series; an ideal voltmeter is infinite resistance in parallel.
topic_guides.analogy: The ammeter is an invisible link in the path; the voltmeter observes across the component without drawing current.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Describe the correct connections for measuring current through and p.d. across a resistor.
worked_solution_steps: Insert the ammeter in series with the resistor.
Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the resistor terminals.
Zero ammeter resistance avoids an added series drop.
Infinite voltmeter resistance avoids diverting current.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not connect an ammeter in parallel across a supply.
checklist: An ideal ammeter has zero resistance and is connected in series to measure branch current without changing it.
An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance and is connected in parallel to measure p.d. without drawing current.
These are ideal assumptions used unless non-ideal meter resistance is stated.

topic_guides.essence: The graph axes determine whether the gradient represents resistance or its reciprocal.
topic_guides.analogy: Swapping horizontal and vertical axes turns a ratio into its reciprocal.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An I-against-V graph has gradient 0.25 A V⁻¹. Find R and the reversed-axis gradient.
worked_solution_steps: For I against V, gradient = I/V = 1/R.
For V against I, gradient = V/I.
The reversed gradient is 4.0 V A⁻¹, equivalent to 4.0 Ω.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not label a gradient as resistance without checking the vertical axis.
checklist: Read which quantity is on the horizontal axis before interpreting a characteristic graph.
For an ohmic component, an I-against-V gradient is I/V = 1/R, whereas a V-against-I gradient is V/I = R.
Exchanging axes produces reciprocal numerical gradients for the same relationship.

topic_guides.essence: Separate resistance due to specimen geometry from resistivity, which characterises the material at a stated temperature.
topic_guides.analogy: A longer or narrower route makes charge flow harder; resistivity describes how resistant the material itself is before geometry is considered.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A wire has resistance 3.0 Ω, length 2.0 m and diameter 0.40 mm. Calculate resistivity.
worked_solution_steps: Convert diameter: d = 0.40 × 10⁻³ m.
Area A = πd²/4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m².
ρ = 1.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m, to two significant figures.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use diameter as cross-sectional area or forget that diameter is squared in A = πd²/4.
checklist: Resistivity is a material property defined by ρ = RA/L, so R = ρL/A. Its SI unit is Ω m.
For a uniform wire of the same material at constant temperature, resistance increases with length and decreases with cross-sectional area.
Use cross-sectional area, not surface area. For a circular wire, A = πd²/4, and diameter must be converted to metres before squaring.

topic_guides.essence: Temperature changes resistance through the material response, and an NTC thermistor converts that response into a measurable sensor signal.
topic_guides.analogy: A hotter metal is a busier corridor for electrons; an NTC thermistor becomes easier to traverse as it warms.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An NTC thermistor is warmed from 20 °C to 40 °C. What happens to its resistance, and how could a circuit detect the change?
worked_solution_steps: An NTC thermistor has a negative temperature coefficient.
Its resistance decreases when temperature increases.
Place it in a potential divider so the resistance change changes the output pd.
Calibrate or compare output pd with temperature to use it as a sensor.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not apply the positive metal-resistance trend to an NTC thermistor.
checklist: For a metal, resistance generally increases as temperature rises because lattice vibrations increase electron scattering.
An NTC thermistor has resistance that decreases as temperature rises, so it can act as a temperature sensor.
Use a resistance–temperature graph qualitatively unless a calibration is supplied.

topic_guides.essence: Superconductivity is a material state in which resistance effectively vanishes below a critical temperature, enabling specialised applications.
topic_guides.analogy: A normal wire is a rough road for charge; a superconducting path is an ideal track only while its conditions stay within limits.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Why must a superconducting magnet be cooled during operation?
worked_solution_steps: The material is superconducting only below its critical temperature.
Resistance becomes negligible in that state.
Warming above the critical temperature removes superconductivity.
Cooling maintains low-loss current and the magnetic field produced by the magnet.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not state that every material becomes superconducting at the same temperature.
checklist: A superconductor has negligible electrical resistance below a material-dependent critical temperature.

Below the critical temperature, current flows with very little energy dissipation. This AS treatment focuses on the critical-temperature condition; detailed critical-field and critical-current limits are outside the required scope.
Applications include low-loss power systems and powerful electromagnets, provided the material is kept below its critical temperature.

topic_guides.essence: Equivalent resistance follows whether the same current passes through a chain or the current divides between branches.
topic_guides.analogy: Series resistors are extra narrow sections in one route; parallel resistors are additional routes sharing the traffic.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Find the equivalent resistance of 4.0 Ω and 12 Ω connected in parallel.
worked_solution_steps: The reciprocal sum is 0.333 Ω⁻¹.
Invert to obtain R = 3.0 Ω.
This is below 4.0 Ω, as required for a parallel combination.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not add parallel resistances directly; add their reciprocals.
checklist: Resistors in series carry the same current and their resistances add: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + … .
For parallel resistors, the pd is the same across each branch and 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … .
A parallel combination has a total resistance smaller than its smallest branch resistance.

topic_guides.essence: Track the rate and total amount of electrical energy transfer, choosing an equivalent power equation that matches the circuit data.
topic_guides.analogy: Power is the flow rate of electrical energy, while energy is the total volume delivered during the time interval.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 12 V heater draws 3.0 A for 5.0 min. Find its power and the energy transferred.
worked_solution_steps: Convert the time: t = 5.0 × 60 = 300 s.
State the result: the heater transfers 36 W and 1.08 × 10⁴ J in five minutes.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use minutes in E = IVt, and do not confuse power in watts with energy in joules.
checklist: Electrical energy transferred in a circuit is E = IVt, where I is current, V is potential difference and t is time.

Use the equation whose measured quantities are known, and keep energy in joules, power in watts, current in amperes, voltage in volts and resistance in ohms.

topic_guides.essence: Circuit values are determined by topology: series paths share current, while parallel branches share pd.
topic_guides.analogy: A single road carries the same traffic through each section; at a junction traffic divides between parallel roads.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 12 V supply is connected to 2.0 Ω and 4.0 Ω in series. Find current and pd across 4.0 Ω. Then state the emf and effective internal resistance of four identical 1.5 V cells, each of internal resistance 0.40 Ω, connected in parallel.
worked_solution_steps: I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A and is the same through both resistors.
The remaining 4.0 V is across 2.0 Ω, confirming pds add to 12 V.
For four identical cells in parallel, emf = 1.5 V and r_eff = 0.40/4 = 0.10 Ω; the load current is shared equally in the idealised model.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use the total supply pd across each series resistor.
checklist: In series, current is the same through each component and pds add; in parallel, each branch has the same pd and branch currents add.

For cells in series, emfs add algebraically in the circuit direction and internal resistances add. Identical cells in parallel retain the emf of one cell; they share the load current, and an idealised bank of N identical cells has effective internal resistance r/N.
Use V = IR for each element after applying the network rule, and check that cells connected in parallel have the same emf before using the equal-sharing model.

topic_guides.topic_title: Charge and energy conservation in circuits
topic_guides.essence: Kirchhoff reasoning applies conservation of charge at junctions and conservation of energy around loops.
topic_guides.analogy: Water cannot accumulate at a steady junction, and a closed journey must return with the same energy balance it started with.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A junction receives 1.8 A and 0.7 A and sends 0.9 A through one branch. Find the other outgoing current.
worked_solution_steps: Total entering current is 2.5 A.
Let the unknown outgoing current be I.
Charge conservation gives 0.9 + I = 2.5.
Therefore I = 1.6 A.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not apply a loop voltage equation as though it were a junction current equation.
checklist: At a junction, charge conservation requires total current entering to equal total current leaving.
Around a complete dc loop, energy supplied per coulomb equals energy transferred per coulomb in components, so pd rises and drops balance.
These rules provide checks on circuit equations with several branches or sources.

topic_guides.essence: A series resistance ratio converts a supply voltage into a predictable fraction at the output terminals.
topic_guides.analogy: The supply pd is divided like a fixed length of rope split between two people in proportion to the sections they hold.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 9.0 V supply is connected to 2.0 kΩ and 7.0 kΩ in series. Find the pd across the 7.0 kΩ resistor.
worked_solution_steps: The total resistance is 2.0 + 7.0 = 9.0 kΩ.
The output resistor is R₂ = 7.0 kΩ.
Use V_out = V_s R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 9.0 × 7.0/9.0 = 7.0 V.
The remaining 2.0 V is across the 2.0 kΩ resistor, confirming that the series pds add to 9.0 V.
topic_guides.pitfall: Use the resistance of the resistor across which the output is measured, not the other series resistor.
checklist: A potential divider uses series resistances so that the supply pd is shared in proportion to resistance.
For two series resistors R₁ and R₂, the output across R₂ is V_out = V_s R₂/(R₁ + R₂), provided the output load does not significantly alter the divider current.
A fixed resistor can provide a constant fraction of a supply; changing one resistance changes the output pd.

topic_guides.essence: A sensor divider produces an electrical signal whose direction and size follow the sensor resistance change and its position in the divider.
topic_guides.analogy: The sensor is a gate whose resistance changes with the environment; placing the gate on one side or the other reverses the output trend.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An NTC thermistor is the lower resistor in a divider. Explain what happens to V_out when temperature increases.
worked_solution_steps: An NTC thermistor has a lower resistance at higher temperature.
With the thermistor as the lower arm, V_out = V_s R_therm/(R_fixed + R_therm).
Lowering R_therm lowers the fraction of the supply across the thermistor.
Therefore V_out decreases as temperature increases, assuming the output is measured across the thermistor.
topic_guides.pitfall: Never state the output trend without saying which divider component the output is measured across.

An NTC thermistor decreases in resistance as temperature rises; an LDR generally decreases in resistance as light intensity rises. The output response depends on which element is measured across.

topic_guides.essence: Emf is the ideal energy gain per coulomb; internal resistance accounts for the voltage lost inside a real source.
topic_guides.analogy: A battery is a pump with friction in its own pipe: the pressure available at the outlet falls when the flow increases.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A cell has ε = 1.50 V and r = 0.20 Ω and supplies R = 2.80 Ω. Find I and the terminal pd.
worked_solution_steps: The total resistance is R + r = 2.80 + 0.20 = 3.00 Ω.
The internal voltage loss is Ir = 0.500 × 0.20 = 0.100 V.
Terminal pd is V = ε − Ir = 1.50 − 0.100 = 1.40 V.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not call ε the terminal pd when current is flowing, and do not omit r from the total resistance.
checklist: The emf ε is the energy supplied by a source per unit charge: ε = E/Q.
For a source of emf ε and internal resistance r supplying an external resistance R, ε = I(R + r). Equivalently, terminal pd V = ε − Ir.
The terminal pd falls below the emf when current flows because energy per coulomb is dissipated inside the source as Ir; calculations must include r when it is not negligible.

topic_guides.essence: The cell practical turns the terminal-pd equation into a straight-line graph whose intercept and gradient have physical meanings.
topic_guides.analogy: Changing the external load probes how much outlet pressure the source loses at each flow rate.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A V–I graph for a cell has intercept 1.48 V and gradient −0.32 Ω. State the emf and internal resistance.
worked_solution_steps: Compare the graph with V = ε − Ir, which has intercept ε and gradient −r.
Read the y-intercept: ε = 1.48 V.
Take the magnitude of the negative gradient: r = 0.32 Ω.
Report the signs correctly: the gradient is −0.32 Ω because terminal pd decreases as current increases.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not quote the gradient as a positive value without explaining that r is its magnitude.

A graph of terminal pd against current has intercept ε and gradient −r, so both emf and internal resistance are obtained from the best-fit line.

topic_guides.essence: The period is set by the system's inertia and restoring strength: mass–spring parameters or pendulum length and g.
topic_guides.analogy: A heavier cart or a longer pendulum takes a slower rhythmic step, while a stiffer spring pulls the mass back more quickly.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A 0.50 kg mass is attached to a spring of k = 200 N m⁻¹. Find its period.
worked_solution_steps: Use the mass–spring relation T = 2π√(m/k).
Substitute SI values: T = 2π√(0.50/200).
Therefore T = 2π × 0.050 = 0.314 s (3 s.f.).
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use pendulum length in the mass–spring formula or enter mass in grams.
checklist: For a mass–spring oscillator, T = 2π√(m/k), where m is vibrating mass and k is spring constant.
For a simple pendulum at small amplitude, T = 2π√(l/g), where l is pendulum length and g is gravitational field strength.
The period is independent of amplitude only within the small-oscillation approximation for the ideal models; the formulae show T ∝ √m, T ∝ 1/√k and T ∝ √l.

topic_guides.essence: Oscillation is an exchange between kinetic and potential stores with constant total energy in the ideal model.
topic_guides.analogy: A swing trades gravitational height for speed and then trades speed back for height.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: At maximum displacement of an ideal mass–spring oscillator, which energy is maximum and which is zero?
worked_solution_steps: At maximum displacement, the mass is momentarily at rest.
Kinetic energy is therefore zero.
Elastic potential energy is maximum.
With no damping, total energy equals this maximum potential energy and remains constant.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not place maximum kinetic energy at a turning point.
checklist: In an ideal oscillator, kinetic energy is greatest at equilibrium and potential energy is greatest at maximum displacement.
Kinetic and potential energy exchange during each cycle while total mechanical energy remains constant without damping.

For a mass–spring oscillator with amplitude A, elastic potential energy is proportional to x² and kinetic energy is proportional to A² − x². Against displacement, the potential-energy curve is U-shaped, the kinetic-energy curve is inverted, and total energy is horizontal. Against time, kinetic and potential energy vary as complementary squared sinusoidal curves and repeat twice per displacement cycle, while total energy remains constant in the ideal model.

topic_guides.essence: Damping removes energy from an oscillating system and reduces its amplitude over time.
topic_guides.analogy: A swing loses height each pass because air resistance and friction take energy.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A pendulum is placed in oil and its amplitude falls rapidly. What has the oil changed?
worked_solution_steps: Oil increases resistive forces on the moving pendulum.
More mechanical energy is transferred to the surroundings per cycle.
Amplitude therefore decreases faster with time.
The motion may become heavily damped and return to equilibrium without many oscillations.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not say damping changes the equilibrium position; it primarily removes oscillation energy.
checklist: Damping transfers mechanical energy from an oscillator to its surroundings through friction or drag.
The amplitude and total mechanical energy decrease with time.
Weak damping allows many oscillations, while sufficiently strong damping can prevent an oscillatory overshoot.

topic_guides.analogy: Timing ten heartbeats rather than one gives a more trustworthy estimate of the average beat period.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A pendulum makes 20 oscillations in 31.6 s at l = 0.25 m. Calculate T and T².
worked_solution_steps: The measured time is for 20 cycles, so T = 31.6/20 = 1.58 s.
Square the period: T² = (1.58)² = 2.4964 s².
Round consistently: T = 1.58 s and T² = 2.50 s².
Plot this point with other lengths to test whether T² is proportional to l.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use the time for all oscillations as T, and do not vary more than one independent variable at a time.

Measure several periods and divide by the number of oscillations to reduce reaction-time uncertainty; repeat readings and control amplitude.

topic_guides.essence: Free motion follows the system's natural frequency; forced motion follows an imposed frequency and may become resonant.
topic_guides.analogy: A plucked guitar string chooses its own pitch, whereas a child on a swing can be driven by pushes at chosen intervals.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A tuning fork is struck and then left alone. Is its motion free or forced? What sets its frequency?
worked_solution_steps: After the strike there is no continuing periodic external force.
The motion is therefore a free vibration.
Its frequency is approximately the tuning fork's natural frequency.
Air resistance may damp the amplitude, but it does not provide the periodic drive.
topic_guides.pitfall: A vibration is not forced merely because an initial force started it; forcing requires a continuing periodic driver.
checklist: A free vibration occurs when a system is displaced and then allowed to oscillate at its natural frequency without a continuing periodic driver.
A forced vibration is maintained by an external periodic driving force; after transients, the system oscillates at the driving frequency.
The amplitude of a forced vibration depends on the driving frequency, damping and strength of the driver.

topic_guides.essence: Resonance is efficient energy transfer at frequency matching; damping controls both the size and sharpness of the response.
topic_guides.analogy: Pushing a swing in rhythm builds height, but friction makes mistimed pushes less effective and suppresses the peak.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Two resonance curves have the same natural frequency. Curve B is lower and wider than curve A. Which system is more heavily damped?
worked_solution_steps: Damping reduces the maximum response amplitude.
Damping also broadens the frequency range over which the response is significant.
Curve B is both lower and wider than curve A.
Therefore curve B represents the more heavily damped system.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not claim damping increases the resonant amplitude; it reduces the peak response in this model.
checklist: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency, producing a large response amplitude.
Damping removes energy from the oscillator. Greater damping lowers the maximum amplitude and makes the resonance curve broader and less sharp.
A lightly damped system has a high, narrow resonance peak; a heavily damped system has a lower, wider response.

topic_guides.essence: Resonance explains strong response when a driving frequency matches a natural mode; stationary-wave formation additionally depends on superposition and boundaries.
topic_guides.analogy: A radio selects one station by responding strongly to its tuned frequency; a bridge or string can likewise select a mode.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A string is driven at one of its natural frequencies and develops stable nodes. Explain why its amplitude becomes large.
worked_solution_steps: The driver supplies energy periodically to the string.
At a natural frequency, the phase of successive driving cycles reinforces the motion.
Reflected waves interfere with incoming waves to form a stationary pattern.
Energy transfer is efficient, so antinode amplitude becomes large until damping balances input energy.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not call every stationary wave or large oscillation resonance: identify a periodic driver and frequency matching with a natural mode.
checklist: In a mechanical system, resonance can produce very large oscillations when an external frequency matches the natural frequency.
Stationary-wave situations may involve resonance when a periodic driver excites a natural mode; stationary waves themselves are formed by superposition and boundary conditions.

topic_guides.essence: Wave descriptions separate size, timing, spatial repetition, propagation and relative position in a cycle.
topic_guides.analogy: For a repeating crowd wave, amplitude is how high people rise, frequency is how often waves pass, and wavelength is the spacing between crests.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Two points on a wave are separated by 0.25λ. Identify their phase relationship and state the phase difference.
worked_solution_steps: A separation of one wavelength corresponds to one complete cycle, so 0.25λ is one quarter of a cycle.
The points are therefore not in phase; one leads or lags the other by a quarter cycle.
A quarter cycle is 90° or π/2 rad.
The wavelength itself remains the spatial repeat distance between adjacent points in phase.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not measure from a crest to the nearest trough and call that one wavelength; that distance is λ/2.
checklist: Amplitude is maximum displacement; frequency is cycles per second; wavelength is the distance between adjacent points in phase.
Wave speed is the rate at which the disturbance or energy pattern propagates. The phase of an oscillation specifies its position within one cycle, such as a crest, equilibrium crossing or trough.
Phase difference is the relative phase between two oscillations: in phase means equal phase, antiphase means half a cycle apart, and a quarter-cycle separation corresponds to 90° or π/2 rad.
Numerical phase-difference conversions are practised in the dedicated Phase difference topic, but the definition and identification belong here.

topic_guides.essence: Speed equals the distance of one wavelength multiplied by the number of cycles passing each second.
topic_guides.analogy: If each passing wave crest is one train carriage length apart and ten pass each second, speed is ten carriage lengths per second.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A water wave has frequency 2.5 Hz and wavelength 0.80 m. Find its speed.
worked_solution_steps: Use c = fλ.
Substitute f = 2.5 Hz and λ = 0.80 m.
The wave travels at 2.0 m s⁻¹; this is not the transverse speed of a water particle.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use amplitude as λ, and do not confuse frequency with angular frequency.
checklist: For a progressive wave, wave speed is c = fλ, where f is frequency and λ is wavelength.
Frequency and period are reciprocal: f = 1/T, so c = λ/T.
Use the speed of the relevant medium or wave; for electromagnetic waves in vacuum, the speed is the common constant c.

topic_guides.essence: Phase difference is the fraction of a cycle by which one oscillation leads or lags another.
topic_guides.analogy: Two runners on a circular track can be half a lap apart even though they have the same speed; phase measures that lap fraction.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Two points are separated by 0.25λ along a progressive wave. Find their phase difference in degrees and radians.
worked_solution_steps: The fraction of a cycle is 0.25.
Multiply by 360°: phase difference = 0.25 × 360° = 90°.
Multiply by 2π rad: phase difference = 0.25 × 2π = π/2 rad.
One point leads or lags the other by a quarter cycle, depending on the chosen propagation direction.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not write 0.25 rad for a quarter cycle; the correct angular phase is π/2 rad.
checklist: Phase difference can be stated as an angle in radians or degrees, or as a fraction of one complete cycle.
One cycle corresponds to 2π rad or 360°. A separation of λ/2 corresponds to π rad, 180° or half a cycle.
For points on a progressive wave, phase difference depends on their separation relative to λ, subject to the direction of propagation.

topic_guides.essence: Classify waves by displacement direction relative to energy transport, not by whether matter travels with the wave.
topic_guides.analogy: A stadium wave moves around the stadium while each person moves mainly up and down; energy travels, but the people do not.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Explain why a sound wave in air is longitudinal.
worked_solution_steps: Air molecules oscillate back and forth about equilibrium.
Their oscillation is parallel to the direction in which the sound disturbance travels.
This creates alternating compressions and rarefactions.
Therefore sound in air is a longitudinal wave, although energy propagates through the medium.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not say a longitudinal wave cannot transfer energy; energy transfer and particle displacement are different directions.
checklist: In a transverse wave, particle or field displacement is perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation; waves on a string and electromagnetic waves are examples.
In a longitudinal wave, particles oscillate parallel to energy propagation, producing compressions and rarefactions; sound in air is an example.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in vacuum, and the field oscillations are transverse even though energy propagates forward.

topic_guides.essence: Medical ultrasound uses reflected high-frequency sound pulses to locate internal boundaries and moving structures.
topic_guides.analogy: It is like sonar: a pulse travels out, an echo returns, and the delay reveals how far away the boundary is.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An echo returns 130 μs after a pulse enters tissue. If the sound speed is 1540 m s⁻¹, find the boundary depth.
worked_solution_steps: The pulse travels to the boundary and back, so the measured distance is twice the depth.
Convert time: 130 μs = 130 × 10⁻⁶ s.
Round-trip distance = vt = 1540 × 130 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.2002 m.
Depth = 0.2002/2 = 0.100 m, approximately 10.0 cm.
topic_guides.pitfall: Always divide the pulse–echo distance by two to obtain one-way tissue depth.
checklist: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing; medical systems transmit short pulses into the body.
Reflections occur at boundaries between tissues with different acoustic properties. Measuring the echo time gives depth when the sound speed is known.
Ultrasound can form images and assess motion such as blood flow; it is non-ionising, unlike X-rays, but intensity and exposure should still be controlled.
