topic_guides.essence: Polarisation tests whether oscillations have a direction transverse to propagation and can be selected by an analyser.
topic_guides.analogy: A narrow rail allows a sliding block to move only along one line, just as a polariser passes one oscillation direction.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Two aerials are used for a linearly polarised radio signal. Explain why rotating the receiving aerial can reduce the signal.
worked_solution_steps: The transmitting aerial produces an electric-field oscillation in a defined direction.
The receiving aerial responds most strongly when its conducting elements align with that field direction.
Rotating it makes the alignment less effective.
At a perpendicular orientation the received signal can become very small, demonstrating directional polarisation.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use the intensity formula associated with Malus's law; the specification explicitly excludes it.
checklist: Polarisation restricts the direction of oscillation of a transverse wave to one plane or direction.
Observation of polarisation is evidence that a wave is transverse; longitudinal sound in air cannot be polarised in this way.
Examples include Polaroid material and aligned aerials for transmission and reception. Malus's law is not required for this qualification.

topic_guides.essence: Stationary waves arise from superposition of matched oppositely travelling waves, creating fixed zero and maximum-displacement positions.
topic_guides.analogy: Two equal ripples travelling towards each other can make a pattern whose bright and dark locations stay in place even though each ripple moves.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: At a node, two equal waves meet in antiphase. What is the resultant displacement at every instant?
worked_solution_steps: At the node the waves have equal amplitudes.
Antiphase means one displacement is the negative of the other.
Their algebraic sum is zero at all times.
Therefore the node remains stationary while neighbouring antinodes oscillate.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not describe a stationary wave as a single wave travelling at zero speed; it is a superposition pattern.
checklist: The principle of superposition states that when waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of their individual displacements.
Two waves of equal frequency travelling in opposite directions can interfere to form a stationary wave with fixed nodes and antinodes.

A graphical explanation should use at least four successive snapshots: draw the left-going and right-going component waves, add their displacements point by point to obtain the resultant, and show the same fixed node positions while antinodes change amplitude and sign. Cancellation remains at nodes, reinforcement occurs at antinodes, and the pattern has no net energy transfer along an ideal stationary wave.

topic_guides.essence: The first allowed string mode is set by its length, tension and linear mass density.
topic_guides.analogy: A tighter, lighter or shorter string vibrates more rapidly, as in the pitch control of a string instrument.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A string has l = 0.80 m, T = 64 N and μ = 0.010 kg m⁻¹. Find its first-harmonic frequency.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use the total mass in place of μ; μ is mass per unit length.
checklist: For a string of length l fixed at both ends, the first-harmonic frequency is f = (1/2l)√(T/μ).
T is the string tension and μ is mass per unit length; the first harmonic has nodes at both ends and one antinode at the centre.
The relationship predicts f ∝ √T, f ∝ 1/√μ and f ∝ 1/l when the other variables are held constant.

topic_guides.essence: Different physical systems support discrete stationary-wave modes whose patterns reveal frequency and boundary conditions.
topic_guides.analogy: A ruler clamped at one point supports only certain vibration shapes, just as a string or air column supports only allowed modes.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A fixed string shows three half-wavelength loops. State the harmonic number, then describe what a microwave probe would detect at a node and what a sound-column pattern represents.
worked_solution_steps: Fixed ends are nodes and three loops mean three half-wavelengths fit into the string, so the string is in the third harmonic.
A microwave probe at a node records a minimum field or signal because the resultant amplitude is zero there.
A sound-column pattern represents pressure or displacement nodes and antinodes set by the air-column boundaries.
Use first harmonic as the assessed term; do not rely on fundamental or overtone as if they were required exam labels.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not count antinodes as one fewer than the harmonic number for a string fixed at both ends; here they are equal.
checklist: Stationary waves occur on strings, in air columns and with microwaves when boundary reflections superpose with the incident wave.

For a string fixed at both ends, the first harmonic has one half-wavelength in the length and higher harmonics add further half-wavelength loops; other systems have boundary conditions that determine their allowed modes.

topic_guides.essence: Stable interference needs a stable phase relationship, and the path difference fixes the resulting phase difference.
topic_guides.analogy: Two sets of equally timed ripples reinforce at some places and cancel at others; coherence keeps the pattern from drifting.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: At a screen point the path difference is 2.0λ. Is the ideal interference constructive or destructive?
worked_solution_steps: The path difference is an integer multiple of wavelength: 2.0λ.
The corresponding phase difference is 4π rad, equivalent to zero phase difference.
The waves arrive in phase at that point.
Therefore constructive interference occurs, giving a bright fringe for equal-amplitude waves.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not call all unequal paths destructive; an integer-wavelength path difference is constructive.
checklist: Interference is the redistribution of intensity produced when coherent waves overlap; path difference determines whether the superposition is constructive or destructive.
Coherent sources have a constant phase relationship. A path difference of nλ gives constructive interference, while (n + 1/2)λ gives destructive interference for ideal equal amplitudes.
A laser and Young's double-slit arrangement provide coherent monochromatic sources, producing regularly spaced bright and dark fringes.

topic_guides.essence: Fringe spacing is set by the wavelength-to-geometry ratio in the double-slit arrangement.
topic_guides.analogy: A wider projection screen spreads the same repeating pattern farther apart, while closer source lines make the pattern tighter.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Light of λ = 600 nm passes through slits separated by 0.30 mm; the screen is 2.0 m away. Find w.
worked_solution_steps: Convert λ = 600 × 10⁻⁹ m and s = 0.30 × 10⁻³ m.
Use w = λD/s.
The fringe spacing is 4.0 mm.
topic_guides.pitfall: Convert nanometres and millimetres to metres before substitution; otherwise the spacing is wrong by powers of ten.
checklist: For Young's double-slit interference, fringe spacing is w = λD/s, where λ is wavelength, D is slit-to-screen distance and s is slit separation.
The relation assumes small angles and a screen far enough from the slits for the standard straight-fringe approximation.
Fringe spacing increases with wavelength and screen distance, and decreases when the slits are farther apart.

topic_guides.essence: Interference is a general wave effect, while laser use demands control of the intense, directional beam.
topic_guides.analogy: Several colours make a pattern that spreads at different rates, whereas a single-colour laser gives a clean regular fringe system.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Why are white-light fringes less numerous and less sharply separated than monochromatic fringes?
worked_solution_steps: White light contains many wavelengths.
Each wavelength has a different fringe spacing and constructive positions.
The patterns overlap and lose contrast away from the central region.
Therefore only a limited set of coloured fringes is clearly resolved.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not describe a laser as safe merely because its beam is narrow; concentration into the eye increases hazard.
checklist: White-light interference uses a range of wavelengths, so coloured fringes are visible near the central region and overlap farther away.
Sound and electromagnetic waves can interfere because superposition applies to all waves; phase and path difference determine reinforcement or cancellation.
Laser beams can damage eyes and should never be viewed directly or reflected into the eye; use controlled alignment and appropriate safety procedures. How a laser works is outside this requirement.

topic_guides.essence: The practical combines a visible interference pattern with calibrated geometry to test wavelength and experimental reliability.
topic_guides.analogy: Measuring ten intervals on a ruler gives a better average spacing than judging one small gap.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A Young's-slits pattern gives ten bright-fringe intervals across 42.0 mm with D = 1.50 m and s = 0.25 mm. A separate grating has 600 lines mm⁻¹ and a first-order maximum at 21.1°. Calculate the wavelength from both methods.
worked_solution_steps: Young's slits: w = 42.0/10 = 4.20 mm = 4.20 × 10⁻³ m, so λ = ws/D = 7.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.
Grating spacing: d = 1/(600 × 10³) = 1.67 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Repeat orders or angle readings, estimate uncertainty and discuss the difference between the two values rather than reporting unjustified precision.
topic_guides.pitfall: Count intervals, not bright lines: ten adjacent intervals require eleven line positions.
checklist: The required practical investigates interference with Young's slits and interference by a diffraction grating.
For Young's slits, measure many fringe spacings across the screen and divide by the number of intervals to reduce reading uncertainty; measure D and slit separation s carefully.
For a diffraction grating, record the order n and angle θ for symmetric maxima, use d sin θ = nλ, and compare repeated values or orders with the expected wavelength.
Use a low-power controlled laser, avoid direct eye exposure, repeat readings and compare the calculated wavelength with the source value within uncertainty.

topic_guides.essence: Diffraction spreads a wave after a narrow aperture, and the spread is controlled by wavelength relative to slit width.
topic_guides.analogy: A narrow doorway makes a sound spread widely into a corridor; narrowing the doorway increases the angular spread.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A slit is narrowed while the wavelength remains constant. What happens to the central diffraction maximum?
worked_solution_steps: Diffraction is stronger when the slit width is smaller compared with the wavelength.
The angular spread therefore increases.
On a distant screen, the central maximum occupies a larger width.
The core conclusion is conditional on comparing the same measurement arrangement: increasing wavelength or reducing slit width makes the central maximum wider.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not say a wider slit always gives a wider central maximum; the trend is the reverse.
checklist: A single narrow slit produces a broad central maximum with weaker side maxima because contributions from different parts of the slit interfere.
Monochromatic light gives a regular pattern; white light gives wavelength-dependent spreading and coloured edges.
The central maximum becomes wider when wavelength increases or slit width decreases. An intensity-versus-angular-separation graph is not required.

An intensity-versus-angular-separation graph is not required, and one short exam-action label on each branch.

Monochromatic light gives a regular pattern; white light gives wavelength-dependent spreading and coloured edges.

topic_guides.essence: A grating converts wavelength into angle through a precisely repeated slit spacing.
topic_guides.analogy: A row of identical gaps acts like many synchronised sources, strengthening only directions where all contributions arrive in phase.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A grating has 600 lines mm⁻¹. Find the first-order angle for λ = 500 nm.
worked_solution_steps: Convert line density: 600 lines mm⁻¹ gives d = 1/(600 × 10³) = 1.667 × 10⁻⁶ m.
For first order, n = 1.
θ = sin⁻¹(0.300) = 17.5° (approximately).
topic_guides.pitfall: Invert the line density to obtain d; do not substitute lines per millimetre directly into the equation.
checklist: For a plane transmission grating at normal incidence, d sin θ = nλ, where d is slit spacing and n is order.
Gratings separate wavelengths because each wavelength has a different diffraction angle.
Applications include spectral analysis; operation of a spectrometer is outside the International AS requirement.

topic_guides.essence: Refraction follows the change in wave speed between media, quantified by refractive index and Snell's law.
topic_guides.analogy: A shopping trolley turns when one wheel enters a rough surface first; the wavefront turns when one side changes speed first.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Light enters glass n₂ = 1.50 from air at θ₁ = 30°. Find θ₂.
worked_solution_steps: Take n₁ ≈ 1.00 for air and measure θ from the normal.
Use n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, so sin θ₂ = (1.00 sin 30°)/1.50 = 0.333.
Calculate θ₂ = sin⁻¹(0.333) = 19.5°.
The smaller angle confirms bending towards the normal in the higher-index glass.
topic_guides.pitfall: Angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface.
checklist: The refractive index of a medium is n = c/c_s, where c is the speed of light in vacuum and c_s is its speed in the substance; air is approximately n = 1.
At a plane boundary, Snell's law is n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with angles measured from the normal.
When light enters a higher-index medium it slows and bends towards the normal; on entering a lower-index medium it speeds up and bends away, while frequency remains unchanged.

topic_guides.topic_title: Critical angle and total internal reflection
topic_guides.essence: The critical angle is the boundary value separating refraction from total internal reflection for a high-to-low index transition.
topic_guides.analogy: A ball launched from a deep bowl can escape only below a limiting angle; beyond it, the path turns back inside.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Find the critical angle for glass n₁ = 1.50 to air n₂ = 1.00.
worked_solution_steps: The light travels from glass to air, so n₁ > n₂.
Calculate θ_c = sin⁻¹(0.667) = 41.8°.
Angles greater than 41.8° produce total internal reflection at this interface.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not apply the critical-angle formula for light travelling from a lower-index medium to a higher-index medium.
checklist: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from higher refractive index n₁ to lower n₂ and the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle.
At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary, so sin θ_c = n₂/n₁.
For air as the second medium, n₂ ≈ 1; no refracted ray exists beyond θ_c and the incident light is reflected internally.

explanations: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from higher refractive index n₁ to lower n₂ and the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle.
At the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary, so sin θ_c = n₂/n₁.
For air as the second medium, n₂ ≈ 1; no refracted ray exists beyond θ_c and the incident light is reflected internally.

topic_guides.essence: Fibres guide pulses by total internal reflection, but dispersion and absorption limit bandwidth and transmission distance.
topic_guides.analogy: A polished corridor keeps a rolling ball inside by reflecting it from the walls; unequal routes make a group arrive spread out.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Why does modal dispersion broaden a digital pulse in a multimode step-index fibre?
worked_solution_steps: Different launch angles create different ray paths through the core.
Some rays take a longer zig-zag path than others.
The rays start together but arrive at different times.
The received pulse is therefore spread in time, which can cause neighbouring bits to overlap.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not treat cladding as an optional coating only; its lower refractive index is essential for total internal reflection.
checklist: A step-index optical fibre has a core of higher refractive index surrounded by lower-index cladding, so light is guided by repeated total internal reflection.
Cladding protects the core boundary, reduces leakage and helps maintain guidance when the fibre is bent within limits.

Material dispersion arises because different wavelengths travel at different speeds; modal dispersion arises because paths in the core have different lengths. Both broaden pulses, while absorption reduces signal power.

topic_guides.essence: Excitation raises an electron within the atom, whereas ionisation removes it from the atom entirely.
topic_guides.analogy: Excitation is moving to a higher floor in a building; ionisation is leaving the building through the exit.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An electron collision raises a mercury electron to a higher allowed level but leaves the atom neutral. Name the process.
worked_solution_steps: The electron has gained energy.
It has moved to a higher permitted energy level.
The atom remains neutral because the electron is still bound.
Therefore the process is excitation, not ionisation.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not call every energy-level transition ionisation; ionisation requires removal of the electron from the atom.
checklist: Excitation occurs when an electron in an atom gains energy and moves to a higher permitted energy level without leaving the atom.
Ionisation occurs when the electron gains enough energy to leave the atom completely, producing an ion.
In a fluorescent tube, collisions with accelerated electrons can excite or ionise gas atoms; excited atoms later emit photons as electrons return to lower levels.

topic_guides.topic_title: Electron volt conversion in atomic collisions
topic_guides.essence: The eV is a convenient atomic-energy unit, but calculations with SI constants require conversion to joules.
topic_guides.analogy: Changing eV to joules is like changing currency before combining prices; the value is unchanged but the unit must match.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Convert 4.2 eV into joules.
worked_solution_steps: Use 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Multiply 4.2 by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹.
Keep appropriate significant figures from the supplied data.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not multiply when converting joules to eV; that direction requires division.
checklist: The electron volt is the energy transferred when one elementary charge moves through 1 V: 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
Convert eV to J by multiplying by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹, and convert J to eV by dividing by the same value.
Use one energy unit consistently when comparing collision energy with atomic-level differences.

topic_guides.essence: Discrete spectral lines are evidence that atomic energy changes occur in definite amounts.
topic_guides.analogy: A staircase produces separate step heights, not every possible vertical distance; an atom similarly permits selected transitions.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A transition releases 2.50 eV. Find its frequency using h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
worked_solution_steps: Use hf = ΔE, so f = ΔE/h.
The discrete transition therefore gives a discrete spectral line at this frequency.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not substitute eV directly into hf unless the energy has first been converted to joules.
checklist: Line spectra show discrete wavelengths because atomic electrons occupy discrete energy levels.
When an electron moves between levels, a photon is emitted or absorbed with energy equal to the level difference.
Use hf = E₁ − E₂ with the higher and lower levels identified; the difference may be supplied in eV or J.

topic_guides.essence: An X-ray tube converts electron kinetic energy into a continuous spectrum plus target-specific characteristic lines.
topic_guides.analogy: Removing an inner electron leaves a vacancy like a missing lower stair; an upper electron drops into it and releases a characteristic photon.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Why do characteristic X-ray lines identify the target material?
worked_solution_steps: Each element has a distinct set of inner-shell energy levels.
The energy difference for a shell transition is therefore element-specific.
The emitted photon has hf equal to that difference.
Its discrete frequency appears as a characteristic line that can identify the target element.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not say all X-rays from the tube have characteristic energies; the deceleration background is continuous.
checklist: An X-ray tube accelerates electrons through a high pd towards a metal target; rapid deceleration produces a continuous background spectrum (bremsstrahlung).
Characteristic X-ray lines arise when target-atom inner-shell vacancies are filled by electrons from higher shells, emitting photons with element-specific energies.
X-rays are used for medical imaging because they are penetrating and absorbed differently by tissues; exposure must be controlled because X-rays are ionising.

topic_guides.essence: Photon energy is proportional to frequency and inversely proportional to wavelength.
topic_guides.analogy: Higher-frequency ripples arrive in quicker succession and each quantum carries more energy; shorter wavelength signals are the same idea in space.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Find the energy of a photon with λ = 600 nm.
worked_solution_steps: Convert wavelength: λ = 600 × 10⁻⁹ m.
Use E = hc/λ with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
A shorter wavelength photon would have a larger energy.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use nanometres directly with SI values of h and c.
checklist: The photon model assigns each electromagnetic quantum energy E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is frequency.
Using c = fλ gives E = hc/λ, so shorter wavelength means greater photon energy.
Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and consistent SI units when calculating photon energies.

topic_guides.essence: The photoelectric threshold is an energy-per-photon condition set by the material work function.
topic_guides.analogy: A single coin must be large enough to pass a turnstile; more small coins arriving together do not satisfy a one-coin threshold.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: A metal has work function 2.0 eV. Explain what happens when 1.5 eV photons illuminate it, even at high intensity. In a second case, the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy is 0.80 eV; find the stopping potential.
worked_solution_steps: Each photon supplies only 1.5 eV.
The minimum energy needed is φ = 2.0 eV.
No individual photon can release an electron.
Increasing intensity increases photon number, not the energy of each photon, so no photoelectric emission occurs.
For the second case, E_k(max) = eV_s, so a kinetic energy of 0.80 eV corresponds to V_s = 0.80 V.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not claim a brighter beam always ejects electrons; frequency must exceed the material threshold.
checklist: The threshold frequency f₀ is the minimum frequency required for photons to eject electrons from a particular material.
Below f₀, increasing intensity does not eject photoelectrons because each photon still has insufficient energy.
The work function φ is the minimum energy required to remove an electron; the stopping potential is the retarding pd that just prevents the most energetic photoelectrons reaching the collector.

topic_guides.essence: Photoemission is an energy balance: photon energy pays the work function and any remainder becomes electron kinetic energy.
topic_guides.analogy: A payment first covers an entry fee; the money left over is what the customer can carry away.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Photons of energy 4.0 eV strike a metal with φ = 2.5 eV. Find the stopping potential.
worked_solution_steps: Use E_k(max) = hf − φ = 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 eV.
For an electron, 1.5 eV corresponds to a stopping potential of 1.5 V.
Alternatively convert 1.5 eV to joules and divide by e.
Thus V_s = 1.5 V.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not add φ and E_k(max); the photon energy equals their sum.
checklist: The photoelectric equation is hf = φ + E_k(max), where incident photon energy is divided between work function and maximum electron kinetic energy.
The maximum kinetic energy is related to stopping potential by E_k(max) = eV_s.

topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An electron beam produces rings after passing through a crystal. What conclusion follows?

topic_guides.essence: Photoelectric observations reveal quantised, particle-like energy transfer from electromagnetic radiation to electrons.
topic_guides.analogy: Electrons receive separate tickets of fixed value rather than slowly collecting a continuous stream of energy.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: At fixed frequency above threshold, the light intensity doubles. What changes and what stays the same?
worked_solution_steps: Doubling intensity increases the photon arrival rate.
More electrons can be emitted per second, so photocurrent increases.
Photon energy hf is unchanged because frequency is unchanged.
Therefore maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential remain unchanged.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not say intensity controls maximum photoelectron kinetic energy at fixed frequency.
checklist: The photoelectric effect supports a particulate model of electromagnetic radiation because energy is transferred in individual photons.

Emission depends on frequency exceeding a threshold and is essentially immediate when the threshold is exceeded; intensity changes the number of emitted electrons, not the maximum energy per electron.
These observations are not explained by a simple continuous-wave energy accumulation model.

topic_guides.essence: Every moving particle has a wavelength, but observable diffraction depends on how that wavelength compares with the structure it encounters.
topic_guides.analogy: A long rope wave can bend around a post, while a tiny-ripple wavelength appears almost straight past the same post.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: An electron has momentum 3.0 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹. Find its de Broglie wavelength.
worked_solution_steps: Use λ = h/p.
Substitute h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and p = 3.0 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹.
If momentum increases, λ decreases and the diffraction pattern becomes less spread out.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not use kinetic energy directly as p in λ = h/p; calculate momentum or use a justified alternative relation.
checklist: The de Broglie equation assigns wavelength λ = h/mv = h/p to a particle with momentum p = mv.

For fixed mass, increasing momentum decreases wavelength. For fixed momentum, changing the mass does not change wavelength because λ = h/p; for fixed speed, increasing mass increases momentum and therefore decreases wavelength.
Diffraction becomes less pronounced when the particle wavelength is small compared with the aperture or crystal spacing.

topic_guides.topic_title: Evidence and changing models of matter
topic_guides.essence: Physics knowledge develops through evidence-driven model revision rather than through permanent acceptance of one picture of matter.
topic_guides.analogy: A map is redrawn when accurate surveying reveals a missing road; useful old routes remain, but the model becomes more complete.
topic_guides.mini_worked_example: Explain how electron diffraction changed the model of the electron without making the particle model useless.
worked_solution_steps: Electron detection still occurs as individual localised events, supporting particle behaviour.
The diffraction pattern requires interference, which is wave behaviour.
The model is therefore extended to wave–particle duality rather than replaced by a classical wave alone.
The revised model preserves successful particle predictions while explaining the new evidence.
topic_guides.pitfall: Do not present scientific models as simply true or false; identify which evidence each model explains and where it is limited.
checklist: Scientific models of matter change when new evidence cannot be explained adequately by the current model or when improved measurements reveal a limitation.
Examples in this unit include line spectra supporting discrete atomic energy levels, the photoelectric effect supporting photons, and electron diffraction supporting wave properties of particles.
A changing model is not arbitrary: it retains successful predictions, explains the new evidence and remains open to further testing.
